title: Bringing the Strands Together
summary: Students run one guided challenge through all four strands and explain how each link in the chain shaped the next.
objectives: Complete a guided challenge combining the concept, a prompted solution, an output check and a risk check.
Explain how the system type and prompt shaped the output.

body: This term you learned four skills one at a time. Today you discover they were never separate - they form one chain, from understanding the system to writing a prompt, checking the output, and using it responsibly. Put all four hats on at once.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can complete a guided challenge that uses all four strands.
I can explain how the system type and prompt shaped the output.
I can name one responsible-use choice I made.

terms.definition: Connecting separate skills into one process.
Whether a system is rule-based or learning-based.

sections.heading: One connected chain
body: The [[system type]] shapes what you can expect. The [[prompt]] shapes the output. The output needs a [[triage]]. And the whole process needs a [[risk check]].
Each strand feeds the next - miss one link and the chain weakens.

sections.label: The whole term in one line
sections.heading: Four skills, one chain
sections.altText: A chain of four steps: work out the system type, write a structured prompt, triage the output, then run a risk check.

edges.label: so you know what to expect
so the output is worth judging
so you know what you are risking

sections.caption: Each step only makes sense because of the one before it. **Skip the first and you do not know what the tool was ever going to be able to do.**

sections.heading: Explain the links
body: It is not enough to complete each step; you should be able to explain how one shaped the next.
For example: because the prompt was specific, the output stayed on task, which made triage easier and the risk lower.

worksheet.title: Week 6 - Core - Worksheet | Bringing the Strands Together

questions.prompt: Mia wants to use an AI tool to help plan a class assembly. Put the four links of the chain in the order the lesson says they should happen, from first to last.

items.text: Triage the output as correct, incorrect or unclear
Run a risk check and choose a responsible action
Work out the system type so you know what to expect from the tool
Write a clear prompt to guide the output

feedback.correct: That is the chain: the system type tells you what to expect, the prompt shapes the output, the output is then triaged, and the risk check covers the whole process.
feedback.incorrect: Each link feeds the next - you need to know the system type before you can write a good prompt, and you cannot triage or risk-check an output you have not produced yet.

questions.prompt: Layla is using a learning-based summarising tool on a news article. Instead of "Summarise this article in three sentences, covering only its main argument", she types "Tell me about this". Using the chain from the lesson, what is the most likely knock-on effect?

options.text: The output wanders off the main argument, which makes the triage harder and leaves more risk of using something wrong
The output stays exactly on task, but the tool takes longer to produce it
The tool stops being a learning system and starts working from fixed rules instead
The triage step is no longer needed, because a short prompt always gives a short output

feedback.correct: Exactly - a vague prompt weakens every link after it: the output drifts, the triage gets harder, and the risk goes up.
feedback.incorrect: The prompt cannot change what kind of system you are using; what it changes is the output, and a drifting output is harder to triage and riskier to use.

questions.prompt: Omar has an AI-written summary he plans to put in a class newsletter. Which of these are genuine risk-reduction choices, as the lesson describes a risk check? Select all that apply.

options.text: Taking his classmates' names and phone numbers out of the prompt before he sends it
Checking a surprising fact in the summary against the original article before he shares it
Marking the parts he could not check as unclear and leaving them out until he can check them
Making the prompt much longer, so the tool has more words to work with
Accepting the summary because it is written in confident, well-organised language
Choosing whichever tool gives him an answer fastest

feedback.correct: Each of those names something that could go wrong and does something about it - that is what a risk check is for.
feedback.incorrect: A risk check asks what could go wrong and then acts on it. Length, confident wording and speed do not reduce any risk - confident wording can even hide a mistake.

questions.prompt: True or false? Once you have written a very specific prompt, you can skip the triage step, because a specific prompt guarantees the output is correct.

feedback.correct: Right - a specific prompt makes the triage easier, but it never replaces it; every output still has to be judged correct, incorrect or unclear.
feedback.incorrect: A good prompt only makes the output easier to check. Miss the triage link and the chain weakens, however carefully you wrote the prompt.

questions.prompt: Match each link in the chain to the job it does for the link that follows it.

right.text: Tells you what sort of results you can expect before you start
Keeps the output on task, so it is easier to judge
Decides whether what you got is correct, incorrect or unclear
Asks what could go wrong and picks a responsible action

feedback.correct: That is the whole chain in one table - each link does a different job, and each one hands something to the next.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what each link produces: the system type sets your expectations, the prompt steers the output, the triage judges it, and the risk check decides what to do about what could go wrong.
